title: Edmund and the Will
premise: When estate lawyer Tamsin Marchetti is summoned to read the will of reclusive archivist Edmund Hale, she discovers a document dated five years before his death — a will that legally cannot exist. Twin letters tucked inside, one confessing to an old crime and one promising 'more if you look,' pull her into decoding a ledger hidden in the town library's catalog system, which implicates the town's founding families in a decades-old disappearance. As Tamsin follows Edmund's paper trail, she realizes her own late mother's name appears in it, forcing her to choose between protecting the town that raised her and exposing the truth. In the end, Tamsin publishes the ledger, accepts that belonging built on silence was never hers to keep, and finds a new home among those who choose truth over loyalty.
about_author: Kestrel Nystrom is the pen name of a former small-town paralegal who spent a decade filing wills, deeds, and quiet scandals before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about paper trails, buried secrets, and the people paid to keep them.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She opens Edmund Hale's estate file and finds a will dated five years before his death — impossible, notarized, and addressed personally to her. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into personal dread as she recognizes her own name in the margins.

chapters.title: Twin Letters
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Two letters fall from the will's lining: one confessing to burning the old Marchetti boathouse in 1989, one reading only 'The ledger knows more than I did. Start at card 447.' She hides both, telling no one. The beat: guilt and curiosity pulling against duty.

chapters.title: Card 447
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with a flashback to Edmund alive. At the town library she finds catalog card 447 leads nowhere — until she realizes the Dewey numbers spell dates. The first decoded entry names three founding families and a missing girl, Ruthie Voss, 1971. Beat: exhilaration shadowed by fear of being watched.

chapters.title: The Alphabetized Town
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Tamsin and Councilman Aldous Wren, who requests a 'routine' audit of her firm. His courtesy is a threat; he knows about the letters. Tamsin lies smoothly for the first time in her career. Beat: the cost of secrecy begins to show.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A ledger page surfaces in her mother's posthumous effects — marginalia matching Edmund's codes. Her mother wasn't a bystander; she was Edmund's collaborator. Beat: grief destabilizing into betrayal, then fierce resolve to finish what they started.

chapters.title: What Ruthie Saw
chapters.summary: Ruthie's sister, now elderly, tells Tamsin the truth: Ruthie didn't run away — she witnessed the Voss mill fire's true cause and was sent away to keep her silent. The families didn't kill her; they erased her. Beat: sympathy complicating Tamsin's anger.

chapters.title: The Audit
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He suspends Tamsin's license pending investigation, offering reinstatement if she surrenders the will. She refuses. That night her office is searched — professionally, by someone who knew where the safe was. Beat: isolation deepening; the town closing ranks around her.

chapters.title: The Confession's Author
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Forensic detail reveals the confession letter was written by Edmund but dictated by someone else — her mother, dying, settling accounts. The 'crime' confessed was a cover for the families' arson-for-insurance scheme. Beat: the mystery pivots from whodunit to why-it-was-buried.

chapters.title: Reading of the Will
chapters.summary: Climax, Tamsin's POV. At the rescheduled probate hearing, with Wren and the heirs present, Tamsin reads Edmund's will aloud — including its codicil directing publication of the full ledger. Confrontation erupts; Wren's own father's signature appears on the final page. Beat: truth spoken in the room built to contain it.

chapters.title: Filed Under Truth
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue-like. The ledger goes public; licenses are surrendered, apologies are partial, and Ruthie Voss's name returns to the town record. Tamsin loses her old belonging and gains an honest one — mentoring a young clerk who asks too many questions, just as Edmund once did for her mother. Beat: bittersweet peace.
